title: In the room, on the table — and words that change shape
title_target: कमरे में, मेज़ पर — kamre meⁿ, mez par
goal: Say where things are — and face the form rule that trips up beginners most: Hindi nouns change their ending as soon as a postposition follows them.
bekal: use में, पर, के पास, के नीचे, के ऊपर, के सामने
put nouns into the oblique form, singular and plural
ask and answer where something is

dialogs.title: संवाद — The lost key
dialogs.intro: Ani has lost her key. In line nine she asks something that may have been bothering you since unit 3, and Priya answers in one short sentence that sums up this whole unit.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: No, and it's not in the room either.
lines.literal: no, room(obl.) — in — also — not — is.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Look in your bag. Or inside the wardrobe.
lines.literal: bag — in — look. or — wardrobe — of — inside.

lines.speaker: आनी:

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: When a word comes after it, "kamraa" turns into "kamre".

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Exactly right! You catch on very fast.

notes: **The rule is as simple as Priya says: if a postposition follows, the noun changes form.** That changed form is called the **oblique form**. कमरा on its own stays कमरा; a room followed by में becomes **कमरे** में. ⚠️ This isn't an exception but a rule that applies to **every** postposition: में, पर, से, को, तक, का/की/के, and all the compounds starting with के.

**Only two groups change; the other two don't change at all.** Masculine nouns ending in **-आ** → -ए (कमरा → कमरे, लड़का → लड़के, दरवाज़ा → दरवाज़े). **Any plural** noun → -ओं (किताबें → किताबों, कमरे → कमरों, लड़कियाँ → लड़कियों). The rest — घर, मेज़, किताब, कुर्सी in the singular — stay put. So *घर में*, *मेज़ पर*, *किताब में*: nothing to change.

**The plural oblique ALWAYS ends in -ओं, no exceptions.** This is the tidiest part of the system, so hold on to it. किताबों, कमरों, लड़कियों, लोगों, दोस्तों, घरों — all of them. ⚠️ Note that the usual plural ending (-एँ, -याँ, -ए) is **replaced**, not stacked: किताब**ें** → किताब**ों**, not किताबें‌ों.

**Compound postpositions all start with के, and that के is itself oblique.** के पास (near), के नीचे (under), के ऊपर (above), के सामने (in front of), के पीछे (behind), के बीच (between), के लिए (for), के बाद (after), के साथ (with). That's why it's *दरवाज़े **के** पास* — दरवाज़ा goes oblique because के follows it.

**⚠️ Adjectives and possessives go oblique too.** *बड़ा कमरा* → *बड़**े** कमरे में*. *मेरा घर* → *मेर**े** घर में*. That's why you've been meeting मेरे and आपके since units 3 and 5 without a full explanation. Now the reason is clear: not because they're plural, but because there's a postposition at the end of the phrase.

**A subtle trap: the oblique form adds nothing to the meaning.** *कमरे में* isn't "in the rooms"; it's still one room. The oblique isn't a plural marker, it's a "there's a postposition after me" marker. Confusing oblique कमरे with plural कमरे is the most common mistake in the first month — and the only way to tell them apart is to check whether a postposition follows.

**होती हैं in line eight, not हैं.** The forms **होता · होती · होते हैं** are used for general truths: "keys *always* end up under books". Compare *चाबी मेज़ पर **है*** (the key is on the table, right now) with *चाबियाँ किताबों के नीचे **होती हैं*** (that's how keys are in general). You'll hear this subtle difference often in sayings and explanations.

grammars.title: The oblique form: one table for everything
body: Compare the second and third columns. Only the first two singular rows change — plus the whole plural side.
after: ⚠️ The difference between **पर** and **के ऊपर** is English *on* vs. *above*: पर means touching the surface (*किताब मेज़ पर है* — the book is on the table), while के ऊपर means higher up (*पंखा मेज़ के ऊपर है* — the fan is above the table, on the ceiling).

grammars.title: The house and what's in it
after: ⚠️ **छत** means "roof" **and** "ceiling", and in India it also means the flat terrace on top of the house — for drying laundry, afternoon tea, and sleeping on summer nights. If someone says *छत पर चलिए*, it's a warm invitation.

sections.title: Asking where things are, and answering

blocks.text: The question-and-answer pattern is always the same: noun + postposition + है. You only have to decide one thing — whether the noun changes form.

blocks.title: A quick way to decide
items: **Question one: is there a postposition after it?** If not, nothing changes. Done.
**Question two: is the noun plural?** If so, the ending is **-ओं**. Done — this holds for both genders.
**Question three: is the noun masculine and ending in -आ?** If so, the ending is **-ए**. If not, nothing changes.
Those three questions cover the whole system. In a month you'll do it without thinking, but in the first weeks, really ask all three before you speak.

blocks.text: A consolation. The oblique form takes more beginner energy than any other part of Hindi, and it's also the part that **stops feeling hard the fastest**. The reason is simple: common combinations — *घर में*, *कमरे में*, *मेज़ पर*, *दोस्तों के साथ* — you'll say dozens of times a day until each one becomes a single sound in your head, not two words to assemble. The rule stays useful for rare words, but the common ones stick first.

exercises.prompt: Put into the oblique form, then add में.
Put the words in the right order.

items: The book is in the bag.
The shop is in front of the house.
